These mourning rites for the deceased may consequently point to the correct interpretation of the divine name su-ha, which, in the second cultic tablet studied by Pettinato, receives the offering of ten sheep in the sixth month, i z i - g a r (TM.75.G.2075 obv. VI 22-24). Reading the name as Sumerian, Pettinato understands dsu-ha as "the fisher god." But if taken as Semitic, dsu-ha signifies the "goddess of the Pit"; in Hebrew the cognate noun sahat often designates the netherworld in poetic texts (e.g., Job 17:15).
